rules.statement: When a shared session or state store is unreachable, fail closed with 503 Service Unavailable; never answer 401 or treat the session as missing.
rules.why: A store outage is not proof that the user is unauthenticated. Answering 401 would log users out or send them into login loops, while 503 fails closed without misreporting the cause.
rules.check: Look at catch blocks and error paths around session-store reads and lease operations. Report any that return 401, return an anonymous result or fall through to a challenge.

rules.statement: When a refresh-token lease or lock cannot be acquired in time, fail the call with 503 and never present the same refresh token in a second refresh.
rules.why: With refresh-token rotation and reuse detection, a second refresh with an already-used token makes the OP revoke the whole token family.
rules.check: Look at timeout and fallback branches in token-refresh code for a retry or fallback that sends the old refresh token without holding the single-flight lease.

rules.statement: Make refresh-token refresh single-flight across the whole cluster through a shared lease, rather than relying on an OP reuse grace window or turning off refresh-token rotation.
rules.why: Parallel requests hold the same refresh token. An OP grace window weakens reuse detection and depends on the OP, and turning off rotation gives up a defense that RFC 9700 §4.14.2 recommends.
rules.check: Look for refresh code that runs without a cluster-wide lease or uses only a per-process lock. Also look for configuration that turns off rotation or adds a reuse grace window for BFF clients.

rules.statement: When the provider's discovery document or JWKS is unreachable, serve the last good JWKS for no longer than a bounded TTL and never relax token validation.
rules.why: Availability must not come at the cost of accepting tokens that were not properly validated.
rules.check: Look at JWKS fetch failure paths for a cache with no expiry, or for code that skips signature or claim checks when keys cannot be fetched.

rules.statement: On a JWT with an unknown `kid`, refresh the JWKS, and rate-limit those refreshes.
rules.why: This handles the provider rotating its signing key, and the rate limit stops a stream of unknown `kid` values from flooding the provider with key fetches.
rules.check: Look at key-resolution code for a missing refresh when the `kid` is unknown, or for a refresh that has no rate limit.

rules.statement: Keep the clock-skew allowance for `iat`/`exp` validation configurable and bounded to 60 seconds at most.
rules.why: Some skew between the client and the OP has to be tolerated, but 60 seconds is the family's ceiling.
rules.check: Look at skew options and their defaults for a value above 60 seconds, or for a missing upper-bound check when the options are validated.

rules.statement: Reject a replayed back-channel `logout_token` by recording its `jti` in a shared expiring store and checking that its `iat` falls within a window.
rules.why: Without a recorded `jti` and an `iat` window, someone could replay a captured logout token.
rules.check: Look at logout-token handling for a missing `jti` record or a missing `iat` window check.

rules.statement: Never send access, refresh or ID tokens to the browser: keep them server-side, in a record encrypted with a key derived from the session handle, rather than in an encrypted cookie or a response body.
rules.why: XSS cannot steal a token the browser never has. Token cookies also cannot work with refresh-token rotation across parallel requests, and they write tokens to the browser's disk.
rules.check: Look for tokens written into cookies, JSON responses or headers that go to the browser.

rules.statement: Key session-store records by a hash of the session handle, never by the raw handle, and encrypt their payloads with a key derived from the handle.
rules.why: Someone who dumps the store then gets nothing usable unless they also have the cookies.
rules.check: Look at session-store writes for the raw cookie value used as a key, or for a token payload stored in plaintext.

rules.statement: Issue a new session handle at every login and never accept a session handle from a URL.
rules.check: Look for login code that reuses an existing handle, or for code that reads a session identifier from a query string or route value.

rules.statement: Set the session cookie with the `__Host-` prefix, `HttpOnly` and `Secure`, and default it to `SameSite=Strict`: allow `Lax` as an option but refuse `None`.
rules.why: RFC 10017 §6.1.3.2 says SHOULD for `Strict`. `__Host-` blocks cookies injected from subdomains, and `None` would allow cross-site use of the cookie.
rules.check: Look at session-cookie options for a missing prefix, `HttpOnly` or `Secure` flag, a `Lax` default, or a code path that accepts `SameSite=None`.

rules.statement: Keep login state (`state`, nonce, PKCE verifier, return URL) in short-lived server-side records keyed by random values and consume `state` with an atomic take, rather than in cookies protected by ASP.NET Core Data Protection.
rules.why: Data Protection needs a shared, persistent, rotated key ring and fails silently across replicas without one. An atomic take in a shared store makes `state` truly single-use on every replica.
rules.check: Look for `IDataProtector` used on correlation, nonce or `state` cookies, or for a `state` check that reads the record and deletes it as separate, non-atomic steps.

rules.statement: Accept only allow-listed relative return URLs after login, chosen when login starts and stored server-side, never read from the callback request.
rules.check: Look for redirect targets taken from query parameters at the callback, absolute URLs that are accepted, or a missing allow-list check.

rules.statement: When proxying API calls, forward only to statically configured destinations, normalize paths, enforce method allow-lists, follow no redirects and strip inbound credentials (cookies, Authorization) before attaching the server-held token.
rules.why: This prevents SSRF and stops the browser's session credentials from leaking to downstream APIs.
rules.check: Look at forwarder code for destinations built from request input, redirects that are followed, or Cookie and Authorization headers passed through unchanged.

rules.statement: Forward HTTP requests through YARP's `IHttpForwarder` rather than a hand-written `HttpClient` proxy.
rules.why: `IHttpForwarder` handles streaming, hop-by-hop headers and protocol edge cases correctly.
rules.check: Look for proxy code that copies requests and responses by hand through `HttpClient`.

rules.statement: Validate provider-issued JWTs (ID tokens, logout tokens) with the family's single JOSE stack, not with a second stack such as Microsoft.IdentityModel or the ASP.NET Core OpenID Connect handler.
rules.why: Two JOSE stacks would put two key policies on one OP's keys, which goes against the decision that JWTs are validated only under the caller's stated policy.
rules.check: Look for new references to Microsoft.IdentityModel token validation or `AddOpenIdConnect` in protocol-client or BFF code.

rules.statement: Hold DPoP and client-authentication keys in a separate, rotatable key ring (ideally non-exportable or in a KMS), record the key's `jkt` in each session, and never store the private key inside the session alongside the tokens it protects.
rules.why: A key stored next to its tokens gives no protection when the store leaks. Keeping it apart confines stolen tokens to the host.
rules.check: Look for private key material serialized into session records, or for DPoP keys generated per session and saved with the tokens.

rules.statement: When DPoP or client keys rotate, let existing sessions keep using their recorded key, and keep retired keys for at least the maximum session lifetime.
rules.why: Removing a key that live sessions are bound to would break those sessions.
rules.check: Look at key-rotation code for removal of retired keys before the maximum session lifetime has passed, or for sessions that pick up the current key in place of the one they recorded.

rules.statement: Check the RFC 9207 `iss` authorization-response parameter against the issuer pinned in the login transaction.
rules.check: Look at callback handling for a missing `iss` comparison, or for an issuer taken from the response instead of from the stored transaction.
